column1: TDE protects SQL Server data and transaction-log files {{c1::at rest}}.
column2:
At rest means stored on disk rather than traveling over a network. SQL Server encrypts pages before writing them and decrypts them when reading them into memory. Applications normally keep using the same queries.
Review source

column1: SQL Server TDE encrypts database files using a symmetric {{c1::database encryption key (DEK)}}.
column2:
A symmetric key uses the same secret to encrypt and decrypt data. TDE uses the DEK for database pages and log records. The protected database stores an encrypted copy of that key.
Review source

column1: In certificate-based SQL Server TDE, the certificate protecting the DEK resides in {{c1::master}}.
column2:
The user database stores its encrypted database encryption key (DEK). A certificate in master protects that key. Keeping these locations separate explains why copying a database backup alone is not enough for a restore elsewhere.
Review source

column1: Restoring certificate-protected TDE on another SQL Server instance requires the certificate and its {{c1::private key}}.
column2:
The destination instance needs the certificate and private key to decrypt the database encryption key. The database backup does not supply them. Store their backup securely and test the restore process before an emergency.
Review source

column1: Encrypt client-server traffic with {{c1::TLS}}, not TDE.
column2:
TLS protects data while it travels over the network. TDE protects files stored on disk. A database can need both because these controls protect different parts of the data's journey.
Review source

column1: Without secure enclaves, Always Encrypted performs column-value encryption and decryption in the {{c1::client driver}}.
column2:
The client driver encrypts sensitive input before sending it to SQL Server and decrypts returned values for the application. Without secure enclaves, SQL Server handles encrypted values rather than their readable originals. The driver needs access to the required keys.
Review source

column1: An Always Encrypted CEK is protected by a {{c1::column master key (CMK)}}.
column2:
The column master key protects the keys that encrypt data. The column encryption key performs the actual column-value encryption. Think of the CMK as protecting a key, not directly protecting each row value.
Review source

column1: Always Encrypted encrypts column values with a {{c1::column encryption key (CEK)}}.
column2:
The column encryption key turns readable column values into ciphertext, which is encrypted data. The database stores an encrypted copy of the CEK. The client uses the column master key to recover the CEK for encryption and decryption.
Review source

column1: Actual Always Encrypted CMK material stays in a trusted key store {{c1::outside the database}}.
column2:
A trusted key store holds the actual column master key, for example Azure Key Vault. The database stores a reference to its location, not the private key material. The client needs permission to use the key store.
Review source

column1: Register metadata for an existing external CMK with {{c1::CREATE COLUMN MASTER KEY}}.
column2:
This statement creates a database record that points to a key already held outside the database. KEY_STORE_PROVIDER_NAME identifies the provider, and KEY_PATH locates the key. It does not create a new key in Azure Key Vault.
Review source

column1: An Azure Key Vault-backed Always Encrypted CMK uses KEY_STORE_PROVIDER_NAME = '{{c1::AZURE_KEY_VAULT}}'.
column2:
KEY_STORE_PROVIDER_NAME tells the client which provider can access the column master key. AZURE_KEY_VAULT selects the Azure Key Vault provider. The key remains outside the database, and the client still needs permission to use it.
Review source

column1: In CREATE COLUMN MASTER KEY, {{c1::KEY_PATH}} identifies the external key's location.
column2:
KEY_PATH points to the key in the external key store. For Azure Key Vault, it is the key's URL. The location is metadata, not the private key material.
Review source

column1: Store metadata containing an already encrypted CEK with {{c1::CREATE COLUMN ENCRYPTION KEY}}.
column2:
A trusted client tool creates the CEK and encrypts it with the column master key. The SQL statement registers the resulting encrypted bytes in database metadata. A shortened hexadecimal example is not a usable encrypted key.
Review source

column1: For system key-store providers, CREATE COLUMN ENCRYPTION KEY names {{c1::RSA_OAEP}} as the CEK-encryption algorithm.
column2:
RSA_OAEP protects the column encryption key with the column master key. It is not the algorithm used to encrypt each column value. The client supplies the already encrypted CEK bytes when creating the metadata.
Review source

column1: Within a column's ENCRYPTED WITH clause, {{c1::COLUMN_ENCRYPTION_KEY}} selects the CEK.
column2:
COLUMN_ENCRYPTION_KEY names an existing CEK in the column's encryption definition. That key encrypts the column's values. The name refers to registered key metadata rather than supplying raw key bytes.
Review source

column1: Without secure enclaves, use ENCRYPTION_TYPE = {{c1::DETERMINISTIC}} for Always Encrypted equality searches.
column2:
A deterministic encrypted value stays the same for repeated input under the same settings. The server can therefore match an encrypted search parameter to an encrypted column value. This does not enable ordinary range searches or alphabetical sorting.
Review source

column1: To hide repeated-value patterns more effectively, Always Encrypted offers ENCRYPTION_TYPE = {{c1::RANDOMIZED}}.
column2:
Repeated input values do not produce a stable encrypted value. This makes repeated-value patterns harder to infer from stored ciphertext. The tradeoff is reduced server-side query support without secure enclaves.
Review source

column1: Always Encrypted columns use ALGORITHM = '{{c1::AEAD_AES_256_CBC_HMAC_SHA_256}}' for data encryption.
column2:
This algorithm encrypts the actual values stored in an Always Encrypted column. RSA_OAEP has a different role: it protects the column encryption key. Do not interchange these algorithm names in their SQL clauses.
Review source

column1: Always Encrypted with secure enclaves supports computations on {{c1::plaintext}} inside isolated server memory.
column2:
A secure enclave is an isolated area of server memory. It permits supported operations on decrypted values inside that protected area. This differs from standard Always Encrypted, where plaintext processing stays in the client.
Review source

column1: Create a database master key with CREATE {{c1::MASTER KEY}} ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<strong-password>';
column2:
A database master key protects other keys and certificate private keys within the database. ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD protects this master key with the supplied password. Replace the placeholder with a securely managed password.
Review source

column1: CREATE SYMMETRIC KEY uses WITH ALGORITHM = {{c1::AES_256}} to select 256-bit AES.
column2:
AES_256 selects 256-bit AES for the symmetric key that encrypts data. ENCRYPTION BY CERTIFICATE separately specifies how that key is protected. The data-encryption algorithm and the key's protection are different choices.
Review source

column1: Use {{c1::OPEN SYMMETRIC KEY}} SensitiveDataKey DECRYPTION BY CERTIFICATE SensitiveDataCert; to open a key protected by that certificate.
column2:
Opening a key decrypts it and makes it usable in the current session. For a certificate-protected key, use OPEN SYMMETRIC KEY with DECRYPTION BY CERTIFICATE. Merely knowing the key name does not open it.
Review source

column1: Encrypt a value with {{c1::ENCRYPTBYKEY}}(KEY_GUID('SensitiveDataKey'), @Plaintext).
column2:
ENCRYPTBYKEY encrypts one value with an open symmetric key. Supply the key's identifier, often through KEY_GUID('SensitiveDataKey'), followed by the value. The function returns encrypted bytes rather than readable text.
Review source

column1: For original varchar(20) text, CONVERT(varchar(20), {{c1::DECRYPTBYKEY}}(Ciphertext)) converts decrypted bytes back to text.
column2:
Decryption returns binary bytes, not a value already typed as varchar. CONVERT(varchar(20), DECRYPTBYKEY(Ciphertext)) interprets those bytes as text. Use the original text type and sufficient length to avoid truncation.
Review source

column1: Close an open SensitiveDataKey with {{c1::CLOSE SYMMETRIC KEY}} SensitiveDataKey;
column2:
CLOSE SYMMETRIC KEY removes the key's availability from the current session. It does not delete the stored key or change permissions. A later operation must open the key again before using it.
Review source

column1: SQL database in Fabric uses Azure Storage service-side encryption with {{c1::Microsoft-managed keys}} as baseline at-rest protection.
column2:
Fabric stores SQL database data in Azure Storage with service-side encryption enabled. Microsoft manages the keys for this baseline protection. This differs from manually configuring certificate-based TDE on a SQL Server instance.
Review source

column1: Layer TDE with {{c1::Always Encrypted}} to add sensitive-column protection against database administrators without external key access.
column2:
TDE protects database files on disk. Always Encrypted protects selected column values from database users without external key access. Combining them covers both risks rather than making either layer a replacement for the other.
Review source

column1: For automatic Always Encrypted input encryption, applications pass values as client {{c1::query parameters}}, not ordinary SQL literals.
column2:
A query parameter passes a value separately from the SQL statement text. An enabled driver can encrypt that parameter before sending it to the database. A literal embedded directly in SQL text does not receive the same automatic encryption.
Review source

column1: Standard deterministic Always Encrypted string columns require a binary-code-point collation using {{c1::_BIN2}}.
column2:
A collation defines how SQL Server compares text. Deterministic Always Encrypted string columns require a binary-code-point rule with the _BIN2 suffix. Use the _BIN2 variant of the database's default collation family.
Review source

column1: For non-NULL ciphertext, DECRYPTBYKEY returns {{c1::NULL}} when the required symmetric key is not open.
column2:
NULL can indicate that the session does not have the required key open. It does not prove that the stored encrypted value is NULL. Open the correct key and run decryption in the database that contains it.
Review source
